ak_hard_sea_cliffs.blurb: Hard Sea Cliffs is a steep, salt-water crag on the Juneau road system, the place locals head when the gentler neighboring cliff has been climbed out. It holds 14 routes, mostly bolted sport lines with three set up for top rope. Grades start around 5.9 and climb quickly: a few at 5.10, a few at 5.11, and the largest cluster in the 5.12 to 5.13 range. The wall is steep and pulls on big jugs, underclings and positive crimps. Plan around the tide, since low water keeps feet and ropes out of the sea. Juneau is damp for much of the year, so pick a dry spell.

ak_first_crag.blurb: First Crag is the biggest cluster of climbs at West Grapefruit Rocks, a limestone outcrop on a forested dome north of Fairbanks. It has 14 climbs of mixed style: six sport routes, a few trad lines, a few set up for top rope, and a couple of boulder problems up to about V5. Grades run from 5.6 to the low 5.11s, with a good group of 5.9s, so it works for newer leaders as well as people looking for a short project. The stone is polished and rewards careful footwork on small edges. The walk in from the road is short.

ak_tram_rock.blurb: Tram Rock is a small forest crag in Girdwood, a few minutes on foot from the Alyeska tram, in the Seward Highway corridor south of Anchorage. It has 14 routes split evenly between sport and trad. Most sit in the 5.10 range, with a couple at 5.9 and a handful of harder lines reaching into the 5.12 and 5.13 grades. Expect a mix of good lines and a few poor ones, some routes need a brush to clear moss, and mosquitoes can be thick in summer, so bring repellent. The setting under the trees is quiet and a pleasant spot for a short session.

ak_ramparts_wall.blurb: Ramparts Wall is one of several walls around the old mine workings at Hatcher Pass, in the mountains north of Palmer, where granite is among the few rock options reachable by road in Southcentral Alaska. It is a fairly new wall, with 14 routes that are almost all trad, plus a single bolted line. The grades are moderate to stout: one 5.8, a handful of 5.9s, and most of the rest at 5.10, with two at 5.11. The Big Eddie and a three-pitch line are the best known. At high elevation, the climbing season is short.

ak_north_gully.blurb: North Gully is the left-hand of the two main gullies at Jaw Point, a coastal cliff area south of Juneau at the mouth of the Taku River, reached by boat. It holds 13 routes, mostly trad with a few bolted lines, from about 5.8 to 5.12. The grades lean hard: a few easier climbs, then three at 5.10, four at 5.11 and three at 5.12. Most of the routes are concentrated on the cliff on the left side of the gully, with a lone trad line in the jungle-like middle and a single bolted route on the other side. Its best-known line is a four-star bolted 5.11b.

ak_left_cave.blurb: Left Cave is one of the sub-areas of the Weiner Lake cliffs in the Mat-Su Valley, along the Glenn Highway east of Palmer, in Alaska's main concentration of bolted climbing. The cliff is made of stacked, overhanging igneous pillars and the cave catches sun for most of the day, so summer sessions are better early or late. It has 13 routes, seven sport and six trad, and the grades are steep: one in the 5.10s, about ten across the 5.11 and 5.12 range, and two at 5.13. A few routes stay dry in the rain. Some days it is packed, other days empty. Watch for loose rock.
